item.title: Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema
item.description:
Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has called on the government to take national action on rising homelessness, crack addiction and public disorder, warning that they are eroding quality of life in the country’s biggest cities and cannot be tackled by city authorities alone.

Speaking in an interview with Het Parool and on current-affairs programme Buitenhof, Halsema said the same pressures were affecting all four big cities – Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – and that the government was partly responsible.

“The problems in the big cities are gradually overwhelming us,” she said, calling for “major measures” from The Hague.

Amsterdam has 3,644 recorded people who cause public disorder, Halsema said, though she stressed the number of homeless people is far higher. The most recent count, in 2024, recorded more than 15,000 people in the Amsterdam region as homeless or at risk of losing their home, though the city says the true figure is higher.

“Public poverty”
The most visible problems come from a combination of homelessness and crack use, particularly in the city’s parks, which Halsema said was distressing residents and traumatising for the addicts themselves.

She said that debates in The Hague ahead of the budget focus on income and taxation, while cities are left dealing with “public poverty”: the visible result of underfunded services, the housing shortage and a strain on the mental health care system.

She wants the government to structurally improve mental health provision and overhaul rules governing foreign workers.

Foreign workers
About 1,500 of the people causing nuisance come from eastern Europe, according to Halsema, many of them foreign workers who end up losing their housing and their jobs because the two are tied together. Amsterdam organisations have previously helped hundreds return home, a significant number of them crack users.

Employers in the Netherlands are allowed to house foreign workers while deducting the cost from their wages, currently up to a quarter of the minimum wage. Former social affairs minister Mariëlle Paul ended a planned phase-out of that rule last year, a decision Halsema branded “disastrous”.

She wants the rule reversed, faster action against rogue employment agencies, and more money for shelter: of the €13 million she said was made available last year for housing foreign workers, Amsterdam received €2 million, which she said is far too little.

Sleeping outdoors
Amsterdam stopped fining people for sleeping outdoors in June last year and, like Utrecht, now wants to decriminalise it entirely. Halsema says fines only push homeless people further into debt and further from help.

Police have raised concerns about that approach. In a review by the local health service in April, officers said people were coming to Amsterdam because they were allowed to sleep outdoors there, and that police and other enforcement teams had fewer tools to steer them towards help.

With annual budget talks ongoing, Halsema said the government must act: “Enable us to make sure our city is in order and liveable.”

item.title: Psychiatrist apologises to parents over euthanasia letter
item.description:
Psychiatrist apologises to parents over euthanasia letter

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A psychiatrist who co-signed a letter calling for an investigation into the parents of a 17-year-old who died by euthanasia in 2023 has said he apologised to them in 2024, telling the TV programme Zomergasten the letter must have been “incredibly painful” for them to read.

Psychiatrist Jim van Os was one of 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging the public prosecution office to take action in the case of Milou, a teen suffering from depression, anxiety and suicidal thoughts.

“For the parents, it can be incredibly painful to read something like this, and I have also apologized for that,” van Os said on Sunday.

The letter asked prosecutors to investigate the extent to which Milou’s parents and treating physicians had influenced her choice for voluntary euthanasia.

The psychiatrists had never spoken to the girl or her parents and doctors. The federation of doctors KNMG has called the letter “indecent and unacceptable”.

Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.

After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.

The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.

The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the prosecution service.

The girl’s parents have sued the Public Prosecution Service to disclose the names of all doctors behind the controversial letter. A court in The Hague will give its verdict on Thursday.

item.title: Government apologises for harm to youth in secure care
item.description:
Government apologises for harm to youth in secure care

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet has formally apologised to children who have had to live in secure youth care facilities, saying the institutions were unsafe and damaging to those kept there.

“It was not and is not your fault. Nothing you went through in secure youth care was your own doing,” youth minister Mirjam Sterk said during a ceremony on Saturday.

Over the past twenty years, more than 20,000 people have been kept in gesloten jeugdzorg, restricted residential facilities for children who cannot remain in their homes.

Youth in these institutions need permission to leave, can be physically restrained and can be held in isolation.

“If you have done something wrong, you say sorry,” Anne Krijtenburg told broadcaster NOS. She spent months a secure youth facility as a child. “Many people think that the pain inflicted upon us is our own fault. Now it is finally being stated that this is not the case.”

Research by the Forgotten Child Foundation found that 75% of the youth they spoke to developed additional psychological problems in closed youth care.

The government has plans to phase out the facilities by 2030 and replace them with smaller living groups.

item.title: PSV thrash Utrecht 6-1 as AZ stay top
item.description:
PSV thrash Utrecht 6-1 as AZ stay top

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

AZ remained the only Eredivisie side with a perfect record after beating Go Ahead Eagles 5-2 on Saturday, a fourth win in four games that keeps them clear at the top.

Reigning champions PSV and Ajax both won comfortably, but Feyenoord drew against newly promoted ADO Den Haag.

PSV thrashed FC Utrecht 6-1 in Utrecht. Ajax, who scored five against Sion in the Conference League on Thursday, struggled in the first half at Telstar before running out 4-0 winners with a flurry of second-half goals.

Down the table
Feyenoord had to come from 2-0 down to rescue a 2-2 draw with ADO Den Haag in De Kuip. The point was ADO’s first of the season. For Feyenoord it was a second home game this season without a win.

NEC won 3-1 at PEC Zwolle in a game that produced four penalties. Twente won 4-1 at Cambuur.

Willem II claimed their first point of the season in a 2-2 draw with Heerenveen, and Excelsior beat Sparta 2-1 with a late winner in the Rotterdam derby. Fortuna Sittard won 3-2 at Groningen on Friday.

Next weekend brings the season’s first top-of-the-table meeting between Ajax and PSV in Amsterdam, with Feyenoord away at NEC and AZ at Heerenveen.

item.title: Foreign students beneficial to Dutch economy, CPB says
item.description:
Foreign students beneficial to Dutch economy, CPB says

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

International students in the Netherlands more than pay for themselves over their lifetimes, and capping their number would do little to ease the housing shortage, according to new research by the government’s economic policy analysis bureau CPB.

The money the government spends on them – student grants, healthcare, social security – is on average more than recouped, the CPB said, mainly because a growing share stay after graduating and pay tax.

More international students do add to housing pressure in the short term, the bureau found. But over time the effect is limited, because the market adjusts – and how far it does depends on housing policy, not student numbers.

A university graduate from outside the European Economic Area contributes about €243,000 over their lifetime, the CPB calculates, and one from an EEA country €82,500. For graduates of universities of applied sciences, the figures are €117,000 and €13,300.

Staying on
Around 17% of students in the Netherlands last year came from abroad, most from the EEA – the EU plus Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Like Dutch students, they pay only the statutory tuition fee, €2,694 this year, and can apply for student finance under certain conditions.

Students from outside the EEA have no right to student finance and pay the full cost of their courses, so cost the government little.

They are also staying on in greater numbers. Five years after leaving higher education, about one in five EEA graduates and two in five from outside the bloc are still in the Netherlands – roughly a quarter more than a decade ago.

“The longer they work here, the more tax they pay,” CPB researcher Paul Verstraten told broadcaster NOS. Graduates are also finding work faster, he said, partly because of the tight labour market.

Changing course
The study was commissioned by the education ministry itself, now run by D66’s Rianne Letschert, whose approach is more accommodating than the previous Schoof cabinet. Graduates who stay make relatively little use of social security and are mostly highly educated, Verstraten noted, so cutting numbers is not obviously the answer.

In 2024 the Schoof cabinet wanted to reduce enrolment to save nearly €300 million and ease pressure on housing and public services. Five universities warned the cuts would hit the economy hard.

Letschert’s ministry has since left universities and colleges to manage the intake themselves, steering recruitment towards shortage sectors such as engineering and healthcare. International student numbers fell for the first time in two decades this year.

item.title: Amsterdam’s baby raves: families reconnect with toddler techno
item.description:
Amsterdam’s baby raves: families reconnect with toddler techno

August 30, 2026 Hannah Docter-Loeb

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

It’s 1pm on a Sunday, and a line has already formed outside Noorderlicht in Amsterdam. Some attendees are dressed in flowy shirts, glitter patterns on their faces, and sunglasses, as if they are going to a music festival. But it’s not your average festival: it’s a Tiny Grooves family rave. And every parent has their kid in tow (or in a pram).

Inside the venue lies a free glitter bar, craft corner, play zone, and of course, a DJ set. The event is a chance for the young ones to dance their energy out, making naptime even easier. But parents can also unwind with their kids in sight, drink in hand.

Family raves have become a phenomenon over the past decade, most recently with toddler techno taking the world by storm. Tiny Grooves brings a similar concept to the Netherlands, providing a space for parents – and their kids – to dance, socialise, and connect.

“It’s a way to introduce your kids to the music you love, and the scene that you love, at a safe time, in a safe place, and at a time that suits your family,” says co-founder Morgan Andrews.

It originally started as a joke. Andrews and co-founder Samantha Barker had connected in 2020, connecting over their shared experience as Aussies in the Netherlands. They stayed friends, having their first kids within a few weeks of each other. And two years ago, when they were on maternity leave at the same time, they started to “lose their minds” during baby sensory classes and the like.

“They’re very much focused on your kid,” explains Barker. “We felt like there’s nothing really where us parents could really go and share an experience with our kids but have it be more catered.” Not to mention, going out to a festival – which both mothers enjoy – can be tough as a parent. The two wanted to find a way to host events for parents to connect with the person they were before having a kid, without disconnecting from being a parent. And thus, Tiny Grooves was born.

In May 2024, the two printed flyers for their first event, handing them out at parks and putting them in Bakfiets around their neighbourhood. Next thing they knew, they had a sold-out event, an equal mix of Dutchies and internationals just looking for a chance to groove with their kids.

Since then, Tiny Grooves has grown: Sunday’s event sold out all 600 tickets (priced at €18 per adult, €9 per kid, and free for those under 18 months). Some parents were hoping to just get at the door – one joking that securing tickets for this was “harder than tickets for Beyoncé.”

Yuri (who wished not to disclose his last name) was one of the lucky ones to score tickets. He used to go to many adult-only festivals, but this has slowed since having kids.

“I was drawn to this idea of having a parent meetup with a good background atmosphere and kids experience,” he says, feeding a bottle to his eight-month-old son in a Baby Bjorn. “I hope the kids catch on because it’s my fave music.”

Karlijn de Koning Strik emphasises that she has not stopped going to festivals since having a kid. But her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter always sees Strik dress up for festivals and feels left out. “Now, we can bring her too,” she jokes. “It’s nice to have a party altogether with the whole family.”

Damien and Manuela Rast appreciated the event for a different reason. Based in Zurich, they spend a few weeks each year in Amsterdam to assess whether they want to move to the city long-term with their five-and-a-half-year-old daughter.

When they saw the event advertised online, they thought it could be a great opportunity to connect with parents in Amsterdam, while still having their child by their side. It was also fitting for their daughter, who loves dancing, and immediately dragged her parents to the glitter bar.

Barker and Andrews are not sure when the next one will be: they have full-time jobs and see themselves as parents first, and family rave organisers second. But it’s clear that when they do, they will have a willing audience.

“This is the format I’m looking for,” says Damien Rast. “Most things are children’s activities or adult activities, but we’re parents with a child, and this is a perfect mix.”

item.title: Dutch women lose hockey World Cup final to Argentina
item.description:
Dutch women lose hockey World Cup final to Argentina

August 30, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch women’s hockey team have lost the World Cup final, beaten by Argentina in a shoot-out at the Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen on Saturday.
The match finished 1-1, and Argentina then won the shoot-out 3-1 to take the title.

The result denied the Netherlands, the nine-time and reigning world champions, the chance to become the first nation to win four World Cups in a row. They played the final unbeaten in their previous 38 matches.

Yibbi Jansen had put Oranje ahead just before half-time, her eighth goal of the tournament as its top scorer. But Maria Granatto levelled from a penalty-corner move six minutes from time, and in the shoot-out only Marijn Veen scored for the hosts.

The defeat ended a run of 35 wins in those 38 games. The Dutch team’s last loss, some 18 months ago, also came against Argentina, who now win their third world title after 2002 and 2010.

“Bitter, very bitter,” said the national coach, Raoul Ehren. Jansen said she could not take in the outcome: “I just can’t believe it turned out this way.”

The Dutch men’s team had already missed out on a home final, losing their semi-final to Spain 4-3 on Friday.

item.title: Dutch men out of hockey World Cup as women prepare for final
item.description:
Dutch men out of hockey World Cup as women prepare for final

August 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch men’s hockey team have missed out on a home World Cup final, losing their semi-final to Spain in Amstelveen on Friday, the day before the Dutch women play for the title.

Spain, coached by the former Netherlands manager Max Caldas, won 4-3 at the Wagener Stadium.

The game turned in the final quarter, with the score at 1-1, when striker Duco Telgenkamp was sent to the sin bin for 10 minutes for pushing a Spanish defender to the ground.

With Telgenkamp off the pitch, Spain scored three times to go 4-1 ahead, José Basterra completing a hat-trick. Jip Janssen and Joep de Mol pulled two goals back late on, but Spain held the lead.

The result ended the Dutch men’s hopes of a first world title since 1998. They will play Argentina for bronze on Sunday in Wavre, Belgium, where Spain will meet defending champions Germany in the final.

The Dutch women, meanwhile, reached the final with a 1-0 win over Belgium and will face Argentina at the Wagener Stadium at 4pm on Saturday. Victory would give them a fourth successive world title, a feat no country has achieved.

item.title: Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers
item.description:
Forget Belgian roads, we need to talk about Dutch drivers

August 29, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Our regular columnist Molly Quell drove through Belgium and France on her holiday and has developed some strong feelings about road design. 

I’ve just returned from the most sacred of Dutch annual traditions. No, not early Sinterklaas festivities or a kring party for my mother-in-law’s birthday.

The yearly pilgrimage to France.

Don’t tell the authorities, as they may well take my passport, but this was my first year making the summer trek south to soak up the sun, drink plenty of wine and contribute to the wear and tear on Belgian roads.

In fact, as a childless adult, I don’t often take a proper summer holiday. Who wants to pay three times more to have your vacation infested with irritable parents and their inevitably sticky children?

I usually have my vacation during the school year when the temperatures are better and teenagers are locked up in educational institutions rather than blasting an unending roll of TikToks at full volume at the table next to mine while their parents order more drinks and pretend everyone is enjoying the perfect summer getaway.

But due to a series of unfortunate events, (namely, being at the mercy of the schedules of people who do have children) I took part in the annual ritual of packing up a car and driving many, many hours to spend time complaining about the French in France.

As I rarely have the opportunity to drive around rural Belgium and France, my husband and I decided to make the most of it and tick off a series of “places we’d like to see but aren’t worth planning an entire weekend around.”

Dunkirk. Omaha Beach. Jules Verne’s grave (very cool). Jardins d’Étretat (also cool). Mont-Saint-Michel (less cool and more like the temperature of Satan’s sauna in August).

We saw a lot of things and thus we did a lot of driving. Therefore, I now consider myself an expert on the ins and outs of Western European roadway infrastructure.

It is classist and problematic to mock the Belgians for their accents. It is simply stating objective and true facts when you mock their roads. It isn’t merely the quality of the roads (which can have a sort of deep tissue massage effect) that is bad but how they are designed.

It is as though Belgian road engineers are required to sample every single variety of local Trappist beer before planning an interchange.

Belgian drivers are also unhinged, but in fairness if I had to commute over Mad Max-style infrastructure every day, I would also operate a motor vehicle like I had no regard for human life.

The French are much better drivers. There is plenty to disparage about the French as a nation and a people, but the overall quality of their driving is very good. They do have the tendency to drive a bit close to the bumper, which my Dutch husband suggests they could improve by “having more than six minutes of driving lessons.”

What is confusing about French roads is the liberal use of the term “round about” for any jumble of intersecting roads without a stop light. Roundabouts have a shape. It’s literally in the name. French roundabouts are what happens when the children of drunk Belgian road engineers scribble on the design plans.

At least the French are largely forgiving of cars with foreign plates driving through their convoluted roundabouts Mario Kart style.

Given these experiences, you would think returning back over the border at the end of the journey would be a welcome relief. It was certainly a relief for my jaw, which I no longer had to clench to keep my molars from bashing together, but the Dutch are not without their own problems.

South of the border, there was a general regard for the speed limit. The occasional outlier (nearly always in a BMW) would fly past you in Belgium or France, but mostly people minded the rules.

The second we crossed the border, yellow plates began zooming past us as though everyone had been informed there was only one plate of bitterballen for the party and it would be distributed on a first-come, first-serve basis.

Maybe it is the smoothness of the roads, but Dutch drivers react to the border marker like a cow does to seeing grass for the first time in the spring.

It was very obvious that these drivers had insider information about the country’s wealth of speed cameras as you would see a car zip past on the left, only to brake a few kilometers later to avoid racking up fines.

Hell isn’t a place where the chefs are British and the police are German. It’s where the intersections are French and the drivers are Dutch. And the Belgians waste hours lost on poorly marked roads instead of brewing beer.

item.title: Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo
item.description:
Oldebroek council executive apologises for Kalashnikov photo

August 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A member of the executive on Oldebroek council in Gelderland has apologised for posting a photograph of himself posing with a Kalashnikov in front of a pro-Russian flag. Standing next to him in the photo is a former Almere council candidate for the far-right FvD party, according to the Volkskrant.

Tom de Nooijer, of the local Christelijk Verbond Oldebroek party, shared the image on Instagram after visiting Transnistria, a self-declared, unrecognised pro-Russian region that broke away from Moldova after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

De Nooijer said he had been on holiday in Moldova and travelled to the region out of a “historical interest in the Soviet past”, and went to a shooting range there. He said the trip was private and not meant as a political statement. He is a former presenter of the right-wing broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland.

He initially declined to comment or apologise, prompting anger from opposition councillors. “They fled the violence he is glorifying by posing for a pro-Russian flag,” said Frank van ’t Ende, referring to the 200 Ukrainian refugees the council houses. A ChristenUnie councillor called the photo “shocking”.

Mayor Tanja Haseloop-Amsing told Omroep Gelderland that the council’s executive had been “unpleasantly surprised” by the image.

In a written statement on Wednesday, De Nooijer distanced himself from the hammer-and-sickle flag in the photo, called the visit unwise and apologised to anyone who might have been insulted.
